profiles.meeting_scenario: The planning meeting is for the next internal milestone of a release-planning decision-support tool used by a product strategy team. The team has already implemented basic feature scoring, and now needs to plan a two-week sprint to add dependency-aware release planning based on mined user preferences from product telemetry and survey exports. The context is that leadership wants a demo for the quarterly portfolio review, showing that the tool can account for how interest in one feature affects the value of another feature. The agenda is to agree on what will be delivered in the sprint, how the mining pipeline and planner integration will be divided between the two participants, what data and environments will be used, and what 'demo-ready' means. The expected outcome is a shared sprint plan covering tasks, owners, and timeline for a working end-to-end demo of dependency-aware planning.

members.name: Nina Patel
members.expertise: release planning systems, product analytics integration, stakeholder demos
members.background: Nina previously worked as a senior product analyst before moving into engineering leadership, and she now coordinates between product strategy stakeholders and the backend team building internal planning tools.
members.private_state: She wants a smooth demo for executives in two weeks, with minimal risk and minimal visible caveats; she is especially concerned about anything that could delay the UI walkthrough or require explaining experimental limitations.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'dependency-aware planning,' the immediate deliverable is planner-visible dependency effects in the demo flow, even if the mining is run offline beforehand.
Using the 'preference dataset' means the cleaned analyst-curated export from the last quarterly study, because that is the only version she has seen in prior demos and decks.
If a feature is 'ready for demo,' it should produce stable-looking rankings on the agreed sample portfolio without requiring environment-specific setup or reruns.
A 'working pipeline' for this sprint can include semi-manual preprocessing as long as the final planning screen consumes the resulting dependency matrix end to end.
The sprint deadline discussed as 'end of next Friday' effectively means business-hours completion in time for rehearsal, not a late-night engineering handoff.

members.name: Leo Martins
members.expertise: preference mining, probabilistic modeling, data pipelines, experimentation infrastructure
members.background: Leo joined six months ago from a data platform team and has been building the telemetry-to-model workflow for internal analytics products, with a strong bias toward reproducibility and automated pipelines.
members.private_state: He wants to use the sprint to establish a reusable mining workflow rather than producing a one-off demo artifact, and he is worried about being blamed later if a hand-built dependency matrix cannot be reproduced.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'dependency-aware planning,' the core deliverable is an automated mining pipeline that regenerates dependency estimates from current preference signals, even if planner presentation remains basic.
The 'preference dataset' refers to the latest raw combined telemetry-plus-survey snapshot in the warehouse, because otherwise the dependency estimates are stale and not meaningfully testable.
If something is 'ready for demo,' it means the computation runs successfully from code in the staging environment and can be reproduced on demand.
A 'working pipeline' implies scripted preprocessing, scheduled extraction, and model output generation without analyst intervention.
The stated deadline of 'next Friday' means code can land by end of day and still count, with polish and rehearsal happening afterward if needed.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to deliver 'dependency-aware planning' in the sprint.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the planner demo visibly accounts for a dependency matrix during feature selection, even if the matrix is produced offline or manually stabilized ahead of time.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means there is an automated mining workflow that derives the dependency matrix from user-preference data, even if the demo surfaces the output in a simple or backend-only way.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is domain-specific and sounds precise, so both assume the other shares the same obvious interpretation; each also sees their version as a natural subset of the same initiative rather than a competing definition.

misalignment_points.topic: Which preference dataset will be used
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to using 'the preference dataset' for the sprint and demo.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the curated CSV export from the Q2 analyst study on 48 candidate features, already cleaned, deduplicated, and used in past stakeholder materials.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the current warehouse snapshot that joins the last 90 days of telemetry events with recent in-app survey responses across 61 candidate features.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: There is indeed a widely known artifact called 'the preference dataset,' but different subteams use that phrase for different canonical sources; because both sources are legitimate and familiar in their own workflows, neither thinks to disambiguate.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the feature should be 'demo-ready' by next Friday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the output is stable enough for the executive walkthrough on the sample scenario, with no visible reruns, no environment troubleshooting, and polished rankings on the selected portfolio example.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the code executes reproducibly in staging and generates dependency-adjusted rankings from source data, even if the exact outputs still need interpretation or the UI is minimally polished.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are using a familiar delivery phrase that usually signals readiness, but each applies standards shaped by their role; because both standards are reasonable and adjacent, the surface commitment sounds fully aligned.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to have the 'pipeline hooked into staging.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this includes loading a precomputed dependency matrix into the staging planner so the end-to-end demo path works from login to ranked release recommendation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means the mining jobs run in staging infrastructure and emit dependency artifacts, while planner-side consumption can remain a separate follow-up if outputs are inspectable.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Hooked into staging sounds operationally concrete, but it hides a boundary question about whether staging integration stops at model artifact generation or extends through product consumption; each sees their boundary as the obvious one.
